name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
title: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
answer: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL, and the major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This site tracks 263 Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, a sign of how many tools now sit between a model and a query engine. The boundary between the two is practical rather than strict: a warehouse is usually schema-first and optimised for SQL, while a lakehouse adds open file formats and a catalog over object storage. Both are used for reporting, feature engineering, and increasingly for retrieval and model inference close to the data.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A warehouse or lakehouse runs on three layers: cheap object storage for the data files, a distributed compute engine for SQL and model workloads, and a metadata catalog that tracks tables, schemas, and permissions. Open table formats such as Parquet, Iceberg, and Delta Lake let the same files be read by different engines without copying. Models connect through APIs or protocols such as MCP, and this site tracks 263 MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses. The platform may be fully managed, self-hosted, or a mix, but the pattern is the same: separate storage from compute so each can scale and be governed on its own.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts with ingestion from operational databases, logs, and files into bronze, silver, and gold layers or similar staging zones. SQL does the heavy lifting for cleaning, joining, and aggregating, and version-controlled transformations keep the pipeline reproducible. AI work adds steps: generating embeddings, storing them in a vector index, and calling a model through a SQL function or a served endpoint. Evaluation and monitoring happen alongside the pipeline, because a model that reads from a warehouse needs the same tests and lineage as a report.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance in a warehouse or lakehouse rests on access control, lineage, and audit. Row-level security, column masking, and role-based permissions decide who can query which rows and columns, and every query can be logged. Provenance matters more when a model consumes the data, because a prediction inherits the rights and quality of its training or retrieval source. Teams track where data came from, what transformations ran, and which model version used it, so a result can be explained and reproduced. Risks include leaking sensitive data through model outputs, training on data without the right to use it, and drifting away from the original consent or contract terms.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward fewer copies and more direct model access inside the governed platform. Expect more SQL-native AI functions, better vector support in table formats, and catalogs that track models as first-class assets alongside tables. Open table formats and protocols such as MCP will keep pushing interoperability, so a model can query a warehouse without a bespoke connector. The open questions are cost, latency, and how to keep governance meaningful when models, not people, are the main consumers of the data.
